A deontological approach to what we ought to do takes facts about the rightness and wrongness of actions as basic, and does not try to explain the rightness or wrongness of actions in terms of the goodness or badness of the action’s outcomes.

The third are cases in which there is a huge gap in the goodness of the outcome. Consider a version of the basic trolly case in which there are 1000 people on the track in front of one. Surely one is morally required to turn the trolley to kill the one. But you can let the trolley continue on its path without using anyone as a means to an end.
